title: Chemical Potential of Each Component Has the Same Value in Each Phase in Which the Component Appears
lead: The chemical potential is the partial molar Gibbs energy, and it changes with pressure in one way for a liquid or solid and in another for a gas. Over a solution the vapor gives a handle on each component: its partial pressure links the component in the mixture to the pure liquid.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise and its solution are AI-written, with Bloom level and concept tags chosen by AI.

exercises.prompt: At 298.15 K the partial pressure of component $j$ above a solution is 0.40 times the vapor pressure $\kPstarj$ of pure $j$. How much lower is the chemical potential of $j$ in the solution than in the pure liquid? Give $\kmuslnj - \kmustarj$ in kJ/mol.

answer.hint: Use the relation that links the solution to the pure liquid through the vapor.
answer.solution: From $\kmuslnj = \kmustarj + \kR\kT \ln (P_j/\kPstarj)$, $\kmuslnj - \kmustarj = (8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(298.15\ \text{K}) \ln 0.40 = (2479\ \text{J/mol})(-0.916) = -2.27$ kJ/mol. A component that escapes less readily from the solution than from its pure liquid has the lower chemical potential there.

footnotes.html: The last derivative is taken at constant pressure as well: $(\partial \kG/\partial n_i)_{\kP,\kT,n_{j\neq i}}$, as in Equation 24.3.1.
The enthalpy row should read $d\kHenth = \kT d\kSent + \kV d\kP + \sum_i \kmui dn_i$, which fits the constant $\kSent$ and $\kP$ of its partial derivative.
The Helmholtz row should read $d\kA = -\kP d\kV - \kSent d\kT + \sum_i \kmui dn_i$, which fits the constant $\kV$ and $\kT$ of its partial derivative.

derivations.what: the chemical potential of a component in solution
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 24.3 Chemical Potential of Each Component Has the Same Value in Each Phase in Which the Component Appears

then.why: Equation 24.3.5 holds for any pure component $j$ in equilibrium with its vapor.

steps.cap: A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of the quotient, and $\kPstd$ cancels.
